title: Pamplona, 1521
hook: a cannonball smashes a soldier's leg, and bored in bed he reads the lives of saints

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the middle ages with a mirror: each age's saints show what that age needed. Your line was what does my age need. Today a new block opens: reform, mission and revolution.

A fortress wall, a French army outside it, and a young Basque officer who won't surrender. The others want to give up; he talks the commander into fighting. Then a cannonball comes through, shattering one of his legs and wounding the other. The fortress falls. The French, impressed, carry him home on a litter. He is Íñigo López de Loyola, a courtier who loved fine clothes, sword fights and stories of knights. The world will know him as Ignatius. The place where his first life ended is Pamplona.
screen: `A FORTRESS THAT WON'T SURRENDER.` → `A CANNONBALL.` → `CARRIED HOME ON A LITTER.`

segments.voice: Ignatius told this story himself, near the end of his life, to a younger Jesuit who wrote it down. He speaks of himself in the third person, and he isn't kind to his younger self. First, vanity. The leg was set badly, and a bone stuck out below the knee. He couldn't bear how it would look in a knight's tight boots, so he had the bone cut away and the leg stretched, by his own choice, and bore the pain without a word. That's the man in the bed: proud, brave, and bored. Second, the books. He asked for the romances of chivalry he loved. There were none in the house, only a life of Christ and a book of saints' lives, so he read those. Third, the daydreams. He found himself imagining doing what Saint Francis did, what Saint Dominic did. If they could, why not him? Then his mind would drift back to a noble lady and the deeds he'd do for her. He noticed how each daydream left him afterward, and that noticing would shape his whole life. Fourth, the turn. Nothing outside him had planned this: a war, a wound, an empty bookshelf. Some readers hold a life like this up to a line from Paul, in the Douay-Rheims: "to them that love God, all things work together unto good." Not that the cannonball was good. Ignatius limped for the rest of his life. But the cannonball is where his story started.
screen: `HE TOLD IT HIMSELF.` · `VANITY: THE BONE CUT AWAY.` · `NO ROMANCES, ONLY SAINTS.` · `WHAT FRANCIS DID, WHY NOT ME?` · then, large: `ALL THINGS WORK TOGETHER UNTO GOOD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one saint you know, or read a few lines about any saint, slowly, the way Ignatius did, and notice what catches: one thing they did. Then ask, lightly, what that would look like in your own life. If you pray, ask that saint to pray for you; if you don't, simply hold their story a while.
Pamplona. The fortress town where a cannonball broke a soldier's leg, and a sickbed with nothing to read but saints began the life of Ignatius of Loyola.
Your line: the cannonball. An interruption can open a whole new road. Day eight hundred forty-seven.

howItsDone: Some Catholics keep a book of saints' lives or read about the saint of the day, and Ignatius's own account of his conversion is read in Jesuit schools and on retreats.

chat.says: How does a proud soldier who loved sword fights end up a saint?
options: For Ignatius, a cannonball: stuck in bed with only saints' lives to read, he began to change.
He saw a vision of Mary on the walls of Pamplona and left the army that same day.
His commander ordered him into a monastery after the fortress fell to the French.
